topics.name: Financial accounting: the double-entry system and verification

questions.q: Which error causes the trial balance not to agree?
o: Transposition in one ledger account only
questions.why: A one-sided error makes total debits differ from total credits.

questions.q: A suspense account is opened when…
o: the trial balance does not agree
questions.why: The difference is held temporarily until errors are found and corrected.

questions.q: A sales ledger control account helps to…
o: check the accuracy of individual customer accounts
questions.why: Its balance should equal the total of the customer (trade receivables) accounts.

questions.q: 75 000 new $1 ordinary shares are issued at $3.50 each. How much is credited to share premium?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the popular distractor used only part of the issue price. Separate nominal value (share capital) from premium: 75 000 × ($3.50 − $1.00) = $187 500.

questions.q: Opening trade receivables are $12 000. Credit sales are $80 000, receipts from credit customers $75 000, discounts allowed $1 500 and irrecoverable debts written off $500. What is the closing balance on the sales ledger control account?
questions.why: Closing balance = 12 000 + 80 000 − 75 000 − 1 500 − 500 = $15 000; discounts allowed and irrecoverable debts both reduce what customers owe.

long.q: From the following, calculate the closing credit balance on a purchases ledger control account: opening credit balance $18 500; credit purchases $64 000; purchases returns $2300; payments to suppliers $58 200; discounts received $1100; a contra (set-off) with the sales ledger control account of $900; and a closing debit balance of $250 on one supplier's account, where the supplier had been overpaid.
scheme: B1: the contra of $900 is debited to the purchases ledger control account (and credited to the sales ledger control account)
B1: the $250 debit balance is carried down on the credit side and brought down as a debit balance

long.q: A trader's draft profit for the year was $42 600 and the trial balance difference was put in a suspense account. Three errors were then found: (1) discount allowed of $380 had been credited to the discount allowed account (the cash book entry was correct); (2) a cheque for $1250 from a credit customer had been entered in the cash book but not posted to the trade receivables account; (3) office furniture costing $2000 had been debited to general expenses. Ignoring depreciation, calculate the corrected profit and the original balance on the suspense account.
scheme: M1: error 1: the account shows $380 credit instead of $380 debit, so the expense rises by 2 × 380 = $760
B1: error 2 does not affect profit (it affects trade receivables and suspense only)
M1: error 3: general expenses fall by $2000, so profit rises by $2000
B1: suspense: debit 1250 and credit 760 clear it, so the original balance was $490 credit

long.q: A business's cash book shows a bank overdraft of $3120. On checking the bank statement: unpresented cheques are $2150; a lodgement of $900 has not yet been credited by the bank; a direct debit of $210 for insurance has not been entered in the cash book; and a cheque for $560 paid to a supplier was entered in the cash book as $650. Calculate the corrected cash book balance and the balance shown on the bank statement.
scheme: M1: the direct debit increases the overdraft: 3120 + 210
M1: the transposition error overstated a payment by $90, so the overdraft falls by $90
A1: corrected cash book balance = $3240 overdrawn (credit)
M1: bank statement overdraft = 3240 − 2150 (unpresented cheques) + 900 (uncredited lodgement)
long.ans: Cash book $3240 overdrawn; bank statement $1990 overdrawn

long.q: Explain two reasons why a business with several hundred credit customers keeps a sales ledger control account.
scheme: B1: it checks the arithmetical accuracy of the sales ledger: its balance should equal the total of the individual customer balances
B1: explained: if they disagree the error is located in the sales ledger, so it is found faster
B1: it gives a total figure for trade receivables quickly, for the trial balance and draft financial statements
B1: it helps prevent fraud, as the control account can be kept by someone who does not keep the sales ledger

long.q: State the journal entries (narratives are not required) to correct these errors: (a) $420 received from J. Lee was credited to J. Leigh's account; (b) rent of $300 paid by bank transfer was recorded by debiting bank and crediting rent.
scheme: M1: (b) a complete reversal is corrected with twice the amount

topics.name: Financial accounting: adjustments and financial statements

questions.q: Inventory should be valued at…
o: the lower of cost and net realisable value
the higher of cost and NRV
questions.why: IAS 2 and the prudence principle.

questions.q: Reducing-balance depreciation charges…
o: more in early years, less later
questions.why: A fixed percentage is applied to the falling carrying value.

questions.q: Accrued expenses at year end are shown as…
questions.why: Money is owed for expenses already incurred.

questions.q: Which is the book of prime entry for writing off an irrecoverable debt?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the most common error was to name the sales ledger rather than the journal.

questions.q: Goods taken by the owner for personal use are recorded as:
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some reversed the entries or used the wrong accounts.

long.q: A machine cost $50 000 and is depreciated at 20% a year using the reducing balance method. Calculate the depreciation for years 1 and 2 and the net book value at the end of year 2.
scheme: M1: net book value after year 1 = $40 000

long.q: Trade receivables are $40 000. The allowance for irrecoverable debts is to be 5% of trade receivables; last year's allowance was $1500. Calculate the entry in the income statement and the net figure shown in the statement of financial position.
scheme: A1: increase of $500 charged to the income statement

long.q: A machine bought on 1 January 2023 for $24 000 is depreciated at 25% a year on cost, with a full year's charge in the year of purchase and none in the year of disposal. It was sold on 30 June 2025 for $11 500. Calculate the profit or loss on disposal.
scheme: A1: net book value at disposal = 24 000 − 12 000 = $12 000

long.q: A business sublets part of its premises for $800 a month. During the year ended 31 December it received $10 400 in rent. It paid $3450 for electricity in the year; $280 was owing at the start of the year and $390 at the end. Calculate the rent receivable and the electricity expense for the income statement, and state how the year-end balances appear in the statement of financial position.
scheme: B1: the extra $800 is income received in advance, a current liability
B1: the $390 owing is an accrued expense, a current liability

long.q: A trader keeps incomplete records. Trade receivables were $8200 at the start of the year and $9600 at the end. During the year she received $61 400 from credit customers, allowed discounts of $900 and wrote off an irrecoverable debt of $300. Cash sales were $15 000. All goods are sold at a mark-up of 25% on cost. Calculate credit sales, total revenue and cost of sales.
scheme: M1: add receipts, discounts allowed, irrecoverable debts and closing receivables: 61 400 + 900 + 300 + 9600 = $72 200
long.ans: Credit sales $64 000; revenue $79 000; cost of sales $63 200

topics.name: Financial accounting: partnerships and limited companies

questions.q: If a partnership agreement is silent, profits are shared…
questions.why: Default rules apply when there is no agreement.

questions.q: Share premium arises when shares are issued…
questions.why: The excess over nominal value goes to the share premium account.

questions.q: With no partnership agreement, how are profits shared under the Partnership Act 1890?
o: Equally, with no interest on capital or salaries
questions.why: Interest on loans from partners is 5% a year.

questions.q: X and Y share residual profits 3 : 2. Profit for the year is $50 000. Interest on capital is X $3 000 and Y $2 000, and Y receives a salary of $5 000. What is X's share of the residual profit?
questions.why: Residual profit = 50 000 − 5 000 interest − 5 000 salary = $40 000, and X receives 3/5 of it = $24 000.

questions.q: A company with 200 000 ordinary shares of $1 makes a 1 for 4 bonus issue, financed from share premium. What is the effect?
o: Share capital rises by $50 000 and share premium falls by $50 000
Cash rises by $50 000 and share capital rises by $50 000
Share capital rises by $200 000 and retained earnings fall by $200 000
questions.why: 50 000 new shares are issued free, so a reserve is converted into share capital; no cash is received and total equity is unchanged.

long.q: A and B are partners. A's capital is $50 000 and B's $30 000. Interest on capital is 5%, B receives a salary of $10 000, and remaining profits are shared 3 : 2. Profit for the year is $60 000. Prepare the figures for the appropriation account.
scheme: M1: interest on capital: A $2500, B $1500

long.q: P and Q share profits 3 : 2. R is admitted and the new profit-sharing ratio is P 2 : Q 2 : R 1. Goodwill is valued at $60 000, but no goodwill account is to be kept. Calculate the adjustment to each partner's capital account.
scheme: M1: credit old partners in the old ratio: P $36 000, Q $24 000
M1: debit all partners in the new ratio: P $24 000, Q $24 000, R $12 000
A1: Q's capital is unchanged; R's capital decreases by $12 000

long.q: A company has 400 000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each and a share premium account of $30 000. It makes a 1 for 4 rights issue at $1.20 a share, which is fully taken up. Calculate the cash raised and the new balances on the ordinary share capital and share premium accounts.

Partner S's current account had an opening credit balance of $3200. For the year S was entitled to a salary of $6000, interest on capital of $1800 and a share of residual profit of $21 500. S's drawings were $27 000 and interest on drawings was $540. Calculate the closing balance on S's current account and explain what it means.
scheme: B1: a credit balance is an amount the partnership owes to S

long.q: Explain the difference between a capital reserve and a revenue reserve of a limited company, giving an example of each, and explain why a capital reserve cannot be used to pay a cash dividend.
scheme: B1: a revenue reserve comes from retained profits, e.g. retained earnings or a general reserve
B1: a capital reserve arises from non-trading gains or is required by law, e.g. share premium or revaluation reserve
B1: capital reserves are not distributable by law, to protect the capital available to creditors / gains are unrealised
B1: they can be used in other ways, e.g. share premium to finance a bonus issue

questions.q: Trade receivables turnover in days is…
questions.why: It shows how long customers take to pay.

questions.q: Gearing measures…
o: the proportion of capital financed by long-term debt
questions.why: Highly geared businesses carry more financial risk.

questions.q: Which ratio shows how many days customers take to pay?
questions.why: Trade receivables ÷ credit sales × 365.

questions.q: A business has current assets of $45 000, including inventory of $18 000, and current liabilities of $30 000. What is its liquid (acid test) ratio?
questions.why: Liquid ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities = 27 000 ÷ 30 000 = 0.9 : 1.

questions.q: Profit from operations is $36 000. Equity is $150 000 and non-current liabilities are $50 000. What is the return on capital employed?
questions.why: Capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities = $200 000, so ROCE = 36 000 ÷ 200 000 × 100 = 18%.

long.q: A business has revenue of $200 000 and cost of sales of $140 000. Calculate its gross margin and its mark-up.

A company has ordinary share capital of $300 000, retained earnings of $150 000, 8% debentures of $200 000 and a bank loan, repayable in five years, of $50 000. Calculate its gearing ratio (non-current liabilities as a percentage of equity plus non-current liabilities) and comment on it.
scheme: B1: comment: below 50%, so low geared: interest payments are manageable and the company could borrow more

long.q: A business takes 48 days to sell its inventory and 35 days to collect money from customers, and pays its suppliers after 52 days. Calculate its working capital (cash operating) cycle and suggest two ways to shorten it.
scheme: B1: one way, e.g. hold less inventory / buy just in time so inventory is sold faster
B1: a second way, e.g. offer cash discounts or chase customers to pay sooner / negotiate longer credit from suppliers

long.q: Over two years a business's return on capital employed rose from 12% to 15%, while its current ratio fell from 1.8 : 1 to 0.9 : 1. Analyse what these changes show and advise the owner.
scheme: B1: profitability has improved: each $ of capital employed earns more profit
B1: liquidity has worsened: current assets no longer cover current liabilities
B1: the business may struggle to pay debts as they fall due, even though it is profitable (profit is not cash), e.g. cash used to buy non-current assets
B1: advice with a reason, e.g. improve cash flow by chasing receivables, reducing inventory or raising long-term finance

long.q: A business's credit purchases for the year were $91 250 and its trade payables at the year-end were $10 000. Calculate the trade payables turnover in days (use 365 days) and explain one risk of increasing it further.
scheme: B1: risk, e.g. suppliers may refuse further credit, charge higher prices or stop supplying / cash discounts are lost

questions.q: Contribution per unit is…
o: selling price − fixed cost per unit
selling price − variable cost per unit
questions.why: Contribution covers fixed costs, then gives profit.

questions.q: In absorption costing, overheads are absorbed using…
questions.why: For example, per direct labour hour or machine hour.

questions.q: Break-even output is 1 250.4 units. What should be stated?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): the break-even point was often not rounded up to the nearest whole unit.

questions.q: Marginal cost is:
o: The extra cost of producing one more unit
questions.why: Examiners (2023): few defined it correctly, often leaving out 'one additional unit'.

questions.q: Budgeted overheads are $120 000 and budgeted direct labour hours are 40 000. Overheads are absorbed on a labour-hour basis. How much overhead is absorbed by a job taking 25 labour hours?
questions.why: The absorption rate is 120 000 ÷ 40 000 = $3 per labour hour, so the job absorbs 25 × 3 = $75.

long.q: A firm with spare capacity is offered a one-off order for 500 units at $15 each. The variable cost is $11 a unit and fixed costs are already covered. Advise whether to accept, with one non-financial factor.
scheme: A1: total contribution = 500 × 4 = $2000, so profit rises: accept
B1: one non-financial factor, e.g. regular customers may ask for the same low price
B1: or the order may lead to future business / uses idle staff

long.q: The machining department's budgeted overheads are $180 000 and its budgeted machine hours are 12 000. Overheads are absorbed on a machine-hour basis. A job uses 5 machine hours, direct materials of $140 and direct labour of $96. Calculate the overhead absorption rate, the total cost of the job and its selling price if the business adds 25% to cost.
scheme: M1: absorption rate = 180 000 ÷ 12 000 = $15 per machine hour
A1: overheads absorbed by the job = 5 × 15 = $75

long.q: In its first month a business made 10 000 units and sold 8000. Fixed production overheads were $50 000. Explain why the profit under absorption costing is higher than under marginal costing, and calculate the difference.
scheme: A1: absorption profit is higher by 2000 × 5 = $10 000
B1: absorption costing carries part of the fixed overhead forward in closing inventory, while marginal costing charges all of it in the period

long.q: A product sells for $40 and has a variable cost of $24 a unit. Fixed costs are $96 000. Calculate the break-even output, the contribution to sales ratio and the sales revenue needed to make a profit of $32 000.

On 1 March a business had 100 units of material costing $8 each. On 5 March it bought 200 units at $9 each, and on 10 March it issued 250 units to production. Calculate the value of the closing inventory using FIFO and using AVCO (weighted average after the purchase).
scheme: M1: FIFO: the issue uses the 100 units at $8, then 150 units at $9

questions.q: A statement of cash flows classifies cash flows under…
questions.why: IAS 7 uses these three headings.

questions.q: Goodwill arises when…
o: a business is bought for more than the fair value of its net assets
questions.why: It reflects reputation, customers and other unrecorded value.

questions.q: In a business combination, goodwill is:
o: The book value of the assets
The price paid above the fair value of the net assets acquired
questions.why: It is an intangible non-current asset.

questions.q: Using the indirect method, how is an increase in trade receivables of $4 000 treated when calculating cash flow from operating activities?
o: Ignored, as it is not a cash item
questions.why: More sales are tied up in amounts not yet received, so less cash has come in than the profit suggests; the increase is deducted.

questions.q: A company revalues its land from $200 000 to $260 000. Where is the $60 000 gain recorded?
o: As revenue in the income statement
questions.why: An unrealised revaluation gain is not trading profit, so it is credited to a revaluation reserve within equity (through other comprehensive income).

long.q: Explain two limitations of using ratio analysis to compare two companies.
scheme: B1: different accounting policies (e.g. depreciation) distort comparisons
B1: historical data may not reflect the future / window dressing

long.q: A company's profit from operations was $68 000, after depreciation of $15 000 and a loss on disposal of $2000. During the year inventory increased by $6000, trade receivables decreased by $3500 and trade payables decreased by $4000. Interest paid was $3000 and tax paid $9000. Using the indirect method, calculate the net cash from operating activities.
scheme: M1: add back the non-cash items: 68 000 + 15 000 + 2000 = $85 000
M1: subtract interest paid and tax paid
A1: net cash from operating activities = 78 500 − 3000 − 9000 = $66 500

long.q: A company buys a sole trader's business for $250 000, paid by issuing 150 000 ordinary shares of $1 each at $1.40 a share, with the rest in cash. The fair values of the assets and liabilities taken over are: non-current assets $180 000, inventory $25 000, trade receivables $12 000 and trade payables $15 000. Calculate the goodwill, the cash paid, and the increases in share capital and share premium.
scheme: B1: value of shares issued = 150 000 × 1.40 = $210 000, so cash paid = $40 000
long.ans: Goodwill $48 000; cash $40 000; share capital +$150 000; share premium +$60 000

long.q: Explain the difference between an adjusting and a non-adjusting event after the reporting period, giving an example of each and how it is treated in the financial statements.
scheme: B1: an adjusting event gives evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period
B1: example and treatment, e.g. a customer owing money at the year-end goes bankrupt: the figures are changed (debt written off)
B1: a non-adjusting event arises from conditions after the reporting period
B1: example and treatment, e.g. a fire after the year-end or a share issue: figures not changed, but disclosed in a note if material

long.q: A company's land cost $150 000 and its buildings $250 000, on which accumulated depreciation is $50 000. They are revalued to land $170 000 and buildings $350 000. The buildings have a remaining useful life of 35 years. Calculate the revaluation surplus, state where it is recorded, and calculate the annual depreciation on the buildings after revaluation.
scheme: B1: credited to the revaluation reserve in equity (shown as other comprehensive income), and the accumulated depreciation is eliminated

questions.q: A favourable materials price variance means…
questions.why: Actual price below standard price saves money.

questions.q: A project's NPV is positive. This means…
o: it earns more than the cost of capital
it pays back in one year
questions.why: Discounted inflows exceed outflows at the chosen rate.

questions.q: Which method uses the net present value of future cash flows?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): ARR uses the average investment, not the total.

questions.q: The standard labour rate is $12 an hour. Workers were paid $25 000 for 2 000 hours. What is the labour rate variance?
questions.why: Standard cost of the actual hours = 2 000 × 12 = $24 000; actual pay of $25 000 is $1 000 more, so the variance is adverse.

questions.q: A project costs $20 000 now and returns $12 000 at the end of each of years 1 and 2. Discount factors at 10% are 0.909 and 0.826. What is the net present value?

long.q: A product has a standard of 2 kg of material at $5 per kg. 1000 units used 2100 kg costing $10 080. Calculate the material price and usage variances.

A machine costs $60 000. It is expected to generate net cash inflows of $22 000 in each of years 1 to 3 and $15 000 in year 4. The discount factors at 10% are 0.909, 0.826, 0.751 and 0.683. Calculate the net present value and advise whether the machine should be bought.
scheme: B1: buy, because the NPV is positive (returns exceed the 10% cost of capital), though the cash flows are only estimates

long.q: The standard labour for a product is 3 hours at $14 an hour. In a month 800 units were made, taking 2300 hours and costing $33 350 in wages. Calculate the labour rate and labour efficiency variances and suggest one reason why both might have occurred.
scheme: M1: actual rate = 33 350 ÷ 2300 = $14.50 an hour; rate variance = (14 − 14.50) × 2300
M1: standard hours for actual output = 800 × 3 = 2400; efficiency variance = (2400 − 2300) × 14
B1: reason, e.g. more skilled (higher paid) workers were used, who worked faster

long.q: The budget for 10 000 units showed revenue $200 000, variable costs $120 000 and fixed costs $50 000. Actual output and sales were 9000 units, with revenue $184 500, variable costs $106 200 and fixed costs $51 000. Calculate the flexed budget profit and the total variance between it and the actual profit, and explain why a flexed budget is more useful than the original budget for control.
scheme: M1: flexed revenue = $180 000 and flexed variable costs = $108 000
B1: a flexed budget compares costs and revenues at the actual level of output, so variances show efficiency and prices, not just the change in volume

long.q: A business uses activity-based costing. Machine set-up costs for the period are $48 000 and there are 120 set-ups. Product X needs 30 set-ups for its output of 2000 units. Calculate the set-up cost per unit of product X and explain one advantage of activity-based costing over a single absorption rate.
scheme: M1: cost driver rate = 48 000 ÷ 120 = $400 per set-up
M1: set-up cost charged to X = 30 × 400 = $12 000
B1: advantage: overheads are charged according to the activities that cause them, so product costs and pricing decisions are more accurate
